To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the 1% rule, which has been proposed in Moura et al (2015) and is based on a linear dispersion analysis, is a good estimate of the spectral resolution limit of under-resolved turbulent flow simulations.

the 1% rule can be used to assess the eddy-resolved capability of high-order DG methods for under-resolved DNS and that, in the inviscid limit, it is crucial to treat the different physical modes in a consistent manner.

the '1% rule', originally introduced to estimate the wavenumbers beyond which the numerical diffusion induces an 'artificial dissipation range' in measured spectra, is here adapted to the case of 3D energy spectrum.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the numerical solution of partial differential equations (PDEs) that model turbulent flows.
the development of high-order numerical methods for the simulation of turbulent flows.
the development of a novel numerical method for the simulation of turbulent flow.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the DG approach, in the limit where no subgrid-scale model is used, has a very good potential to be a viable alternative to LES, especially in the case of high-Reynolds-number flows, but that further research is needed to confirm this statement.
, for under-resolved DNS, the 1% rule is not a universal rule.
the 1% rule is a very useful tool for the design of DG-based implicit large eddy simulations of free turbulence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the high-order DG method is capable of simulating turbulence at very high Re, but the numerical dissipation should be carefully controlled.
the 1% rule can provide useful estimates of the eddy-resolved capability of a DG scheme.
the high-order DG approach can be a promising tool for implicit LES or under-resolved DNS in the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 1% rule can be extended to the energy spectra and that it is not necessary to use a very accurate and expensive Riemann solver to obtain accurate estimates.
the 1% rule is not only a useful guideline but also an accurate predictor of the onset of numerical dissipation in under-resolved Euler simulations with DG schemes.
, in the absence of explicit dissipation, the spectral resolution power of DG methods is not limited by the order of accuracy of the numerical scheme, as long as a proper Riemann solver is used.
